facts.text: The service must crawl a list of URLs, build a reverse index of words to pages, and generate static titles and snippets; a user enters a search term and sees matching pages with those titles and snippets.

The service must be highly available and generate search results fast, and the crawler must not get stuck in an infinite loop. Search analytics and personalized results are out of scope, and only anonymous users are supported.
An infinite loop happens if the link graph contains a cycle. Search traffic is not evenly distributed: some searches are very popular, while others are executed only once.

The assumptions are 1 billion links to crawl, a refresh rate of about once per week (more often for popular sites), 4 billion links crawled each month, 500 KB average stored size per page, and 100 billion searches per month.
The estimate is 2 PB of stored page content per month (500 KB per page times 4 billion links), 72 PB in 3 years, 1,600 write requests per second and 40,000 search requests per second.

The data model is two tables: links_to_crawl, ranked initially by overall site popularity, and crawled_links, which stores processed links with their page signatures. Both could live in a key-value NoSQL database, with Redis sorted sets keeping the link ranking.
If the initial list is not reasonable, the crawler can be seeded with popular sites that link to outside content, such as Yahoo or DMOZ.
In a loop the Crawler Service takes the top ranked link and checks crawled_links for a similar page signature. If a similar page exists, it lowers the link's priority, which prevents a cycle.

Otherwise it crawls the link, queues a job for the Reverse Index Service and one for the Document Service (static title and snippet), generates the page signature, removes the link from links_to_crawl and inserts the link and signature into crawled_links.
Duplicate URLs can be removed with sort and unique for small lists. With 1 billion links to crawl, MapReduce can output only the entries that have a frequency of 1.
Detecting duplicate content is more complex: generate a signature from each page's contents and compare signatures for similarity, using an algorithm such as the Jaccard index or cosine similarity.

Each crawl result carries a timestamp of the last crawl. After a default period, say one week, all pages are refreshed, and frequently updated or popular sites are refreshed sooner. A Robots.txt file could give webmasters control of crawl frequency.

A search goes from the client to a reverse-proxy web server, then to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations.

The Query API server asks the Reverse Index Service for matching documents; it ranks them and returns the top ones, and the Document Service returns titles and snippets. The public API is REST; internal calls could use RPC.

Popular queries can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached, which cuts response times, protects the Reverse Index Service and Document Service, and absorbs uneven traffic and spikes.

The Reverse Index Service and Document Service will likely need heavy sharding and federation. The crawler itself can keep its own periodically refreshed DNS lookup, pool many open connections, and needs enough bandwidth, since crawling is bandwidth intensive.

definition.text: An Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads.

facts.text: A crawler starts from a list of seed URLs, fetches those pages, finds their hyperlinks and adds them to the list of URLs still to visit, called the crawl frontier.

Frontier URLs are visited recursively according to a set of policies: selection (which pages to download), re-visit (when to check for changes), politeness (how to avoid overloading sites) and parallelization (how to coordinate distributed crawlers).
The web is so large that a crawler can download only a limited number of pages in a given time, so it must prioritize, and fast change means pages may already be updated or deleted.

Server-side software makes duplicate content hard to avoid: a photo gallery with four sort orders, three thumbnail sizes, two file formats and an option to hide user content serves the same content under 48 different URLs.

A parallel crawler runs multiple processes at once, aiming to maximize the download rate while minimizing overhead. It needs a policy for assigning newly found URLs, because two processes can discover the same URL and download the page twice.
Crawlers typically identify themselves to a web server in the User-agent field of the HTTP request, which administrators read in server logs to see which crawlers visit and how often.

definition.text: The rule that decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking pages by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched.

facts.text: Even large search engines cover only part of the public web; a 2009 study showed they index no more than 40-70% of the indexable web.

The downloaded fraction should hold the most relevant pages rather than a random sample, which needs an importance metric built from a page's intrinsic quality, its popularity in links or visits, and sometimes its URL.
A selection policy must work with partial information, since the complete set of web pages is not known while crawling.
A breadth-first crawl captures pages with high PageRank early, because the most important pages have many links from numerous hosts and those links are found early wherever the crawl starts.

OPIC gives each page an initial sum of cash, split equally among the pages it links to; the crawler downloads frontier pages holding the most cash first. It resembles PageRank but is faster and done in one step.
To fetch only HTML, a crawler can send an HTTP HEAD request for the MIME type before a GET, or skip URLs not ending in characters such as .html or a slash, though that may skip many HTML resources.
Some crawlers skip any URL containing a "?" to avoid spider traps that yield an infinite number of URLs from one site; this is unreliable when the site rewrites URLs.

title: URL normalization
article: Web crawler#Crawling policy > Selection policy > URL normalization

definition.text: Modifying and standardizing a URL in a consistent way, also called URL canonicalization, so that one resource has one form.

facts.text: Crawlers usually normalize URLs to avoid crawling the same resource more than once.
Normalization, also called URL canonicalization, modifies and standardizes a URL in a consistent manner.
Typical normalizations convert URLs to lowercase, remove "." and ".." segments, and add trailing slashes to a non-empty path component.

title: Focused crawler
article: Web crawler#Crawling policy > Selection policy > Focused crawling

definition.text: A crawler that tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic, also called a topical crawler.

facts.text: A page's importance can be expressed as its similarity to a query; crawlers that fetch pages similar to each other are called focused or topical crawlers.
The main problem is predicting a page's text similarity to the query before downloading it; one predictor is the anchor text of links, and another is the full content of pages already visited.
Performance depends mostly on how rich in links the topic is, and a focused crawl usually relies on a general web search engine to supply starting points.

definition.text: The rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale.

facts.text: A crawl of part of the web can take weeks or months, so creations, updates and deletions happen meanwhile, and the search engine pays a cost for holding an outdated copy.
The usual cost functions are freshness, a binary measure of whether the local copy is accurate, and age, a measure of how outdated the copy is.
A uniform policy re-visits all pages at the same frequency; a proportional policy re-visits pages that change more often more frequently, in proportion to their estimated change rate.
In average freshness the uniform policy beats the proportional one, because a proportional policy spends crawls on rapidly changing pages whose freshness lasts only briefly.

The optimal policy is closer to uniform: to keep average freshness high, ignore pages that change too often, and to keep average age low, raise access frequency sub-linearly with a page's rate of change.

definition.text: The rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits.

facts.text: Crawlers fetch data faster and deeper than human searchers, so one making many requests per second or downloading large files can cripple a site's performance.
The costs of crawlers include network bandwidth, server overload when access to one server is too frequent, and poorly written crawlers that can crash servers or routers.

The robots exclusion protocol only partly solves this: it says which parts of a server crawlers should avoid but suggests no interval between visits, though that interval is the most effective way to avoid overload.
Major search engines support an extra Crawl-delay parameter in robots.txt giving the number of seconds to wait between requests.
The first proposed interval was 60 seconds, but at that rate a site of more than 100,000 pages would take over 2 months to download; Cho uses 10 seconds, WIRE 15 seconds and Dill et al. 1 second.
The Mercator crawler is adaptive: if a download from a server took t seconds, it waits 10t seconds before fetching the next page from it.

definition.text: The robots.txt standard through which site administrators tell crawlers which parts of their web servers must not be accessed.

facts.text: Website owners use robots.txt to tell crawlers which resources they may and may not request, and a crawler uses it to decide which links to follow and which to avoid.
The standard has no interval between visits, but major search engines read an extra Crawl-delay parameter giving the seconds to wait between requests.
Owners can reduce exposure by allowing indexing of only the public parts of a site and blocking transactional parts such as login and private pages with robots.txt.
The system design primer suggests supporting robots.txt in a crawler so webmasters control crawl frequency.

definition.text: Search engines work through three processes: crawling pages, indexing what was collected, and serving ranked results for queries.

facts.text: Crawlers start from a list of known pages (seeds) and follow links to discover and download new pages.

The collected information is analyzed and organized into a massive index, extracting keywords, content type, freshness, language and other signals to learn what each page is about and how relevant it may be to queries.
To serve a query, the engine first analyzes it for meaning and intent, identifying keywords, recognizing synonyms and interpreting context.
It then retrieves pages from the index by matching the query's keywords with indexed content, and ranks the retrieved pages by relevance and other factors.

definition.text: Reaching the large share of web pages that sit behind queries to a database and have no links pointing to them.

facts.text: A vast number of pages lie in the deep or invisible web, usually reachable only by submitting queries to a database, so regular crawlers cannot find them without links that point to them.
Google's Sitemaps protocol and mod oai are intended to let deep-web resources be discovered; deep web crawling also multiplies the number of links to crawl.
Screen scraping software can be customized to query a web form repeatedly and aggregate the results, even feeding the output of one form into another across websites.
Pages built on AJAX cause problems for crawlers, and Google has proposed a format of AJAX calls its bot can recognize and index.
